title: Vinod Khosla's First Blunder as Seahawks Owner
htmlContent:
Vinod Khosla's tenure as owner of the Seattle Seahawks had been running smoothly until last week. Then a few loosely chosen words about the franchise's long-term home set off a wave of anxiety across the Pacific Northwest.

Asked about the possibility of the team ever leaving Seattle, Khosla declined to rule it out, leaning on a "never say never" line and a reference to not being able to predict what happens 500 years from now. He later clarified that he wants the Seahawks to stay put. But the damage was done, and the way he handled the cleanup only extended the news cycle.

Mike Sando of <em>The Athletic argued that Khosla could learn something from his own head coach, Mike Macdonald.

Seattle Fans Have Heard This Before

Hedging about the distant future is a perfectly normal habit in the investment world. But sports fans do not think about their teams the way analysts think about a stock. Loyalty to a local franchise is emotional, generational, and tied to identity.

That is especially true in Seattle, where the wound left by the SuperSonics' move to Oklahoma City in 2008 has never fully healed. A city that watched one beloved franchise pack up and leave does not hear "never say never" as harmless philosophy. It hears a warning.

Rather than acknowledging that sensitivity, Khosla went on offense. He took aim at reporters, accusing them of chasing clicks, distorting his answer, and sending the city into a spiral for no reason. His intended message—that the team is staying—got buried.

What Mike Macdonald Did Differently

Macdonald had his own misstep recently. In a conversation with Graham Bensinger, the Seahawks head coach revealed that Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton nearly accused Seattle of cheating during the 2024 season. The Seahawks had found clips of Broncos practices posted online and used them in their preparation. According to Macdonald, the situation turned into a quiet standoff, with Seattle prepared to pursue legal action if Payton went public with the accusation.

It was not a story Macdonald needed to tell, and he recognized that quickly. He apologized soon after the clip circulated and owned the lapse in judgment without blaming anyone else.

That is the contrast Sando highlighted. In his view, Khosla could have defused everything with a short, humble acknowledgment that words matter, a promise to choose his more carefully, and a reaffirmation that the Seahawks belong in Seattle. Instead, the owner doubled down.

A Steelers Fan Who Should Study the Steelers

Khosla introduced himself to Seattle as a Pittsburgh Steelers fan, and he previously held a minority stake in the San Francisco 49ers, a division rival. Fans understand this is a business investment, but the lack of a deep connection to the region has bred skepticism, and relocation talk only adds to it.

One NFL executive who spoke with Sando pointed out the irony. If Khosla admires the Steelers, the executive suggested, he should look closely at how that organization operates and ask why it works. The executive also pushed back on the idea that the media twisted anything, noting that Khosla said the words himself.

Pittsburgh has long kept its public profile modest, letting results do the talking. The Allen family rarely engaged with the media during its ownership, and general manager John Schneider and Macdonald have no interest in becoming the story. Their focus is winning.

Vinod Khosla Must Develop as an Owner Before Inevitable Team Struggles

Khosla has shown little interest in softening his approach. In his follow-up, he said he dislikes the pretense of media training, prefers to say things as they are, and will not tolerate what he considers bad reporting. He even compared the relocation question to his political views, saying he would never say never about supporting Donald Trump, however unlikely, before repeating that he cannot predict 500 years out and stays true to his style.

Authenticity has value, but this response created more confusion than clarity. Sometimes the best statement is a brief one, or none at all. Running an NFL franchise often means setting aside personal preferences for the good of the team and the city that supports it.

Khosla's record as a business leader suggests he is capable of adapting. The open question is how quickly. The Seahawks are coming off a Super Bowl-winning season and are among the best-run organizations in the league. They do not need an owner turning routine questions into controversies.

The executive who spoke to Sando raised the concern that should linger most. This flare-up happened while the team is winning. When the losing comes, scrutiny on ownership will intensify. As the executive noted, drawing attention to yourself has rarely served any owner well.

Khosla's first stumble does not define his ownership. But it should serve as an early lesson—one his own head coach has already demonstrated: own the mistake, keep it short, and get back to the business of winning.
excerpt: Vinod Khosla's "never say never" comment about the Seahawks' long-term home in Seattle sparked a wave of anxiety across the Pacific Northwest, and his combative response only extended the controversy, drawing a sharp contrast with head coach Mike Macdonald's handling of his own recent misstep.
